entries.067b399bd7d4e41104c0281f8732a592ddf93ef5: <div sID="gen10190" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="38" osisID="Job.38" sID="Job.38"/> <div eID="gen10190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10191" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10192" type="x-p"/> In most disputes the strife is who shall have the last word. Job's friends had, in this controversy, tamely yielded it to Job, and then he to Elihu. But, after all the wranglings of the counsel at bar, the judge upon the bench must have the last word; so God had here, and so he will have in every controversy, for every man's judgment proceeds from him and by his definitive sentence every man must stand or fall and every cause be won or lost. Job had often appealed to God, and had talked boldly how he would order his cause before him, and as a prince would he go near unto him; but, when God took the throne, Job had nothing to say in his own defence, but was silent before him. It is not so easy a matter as some think it to contest with the Almighty. Job's friends had sometimes appealed to God too: "O that God would speak!" <reference osisRef="Job.11.7">ch. xi. 7</reference>. And now, at length, God does speak, when Job, by Elihu's clear and close arguings was mollified a little, and mortified, and so prepared to hear what God had to say. It is the office of ministers to prepare the way of the Lord. That which the great God designs in this discourse is to humble Job, and bring him to repent of, and to recant, his passionate indecent expressions concerning God's providential dealings with him; and this he does by calling upon Job to compare God's eternity with his own time, God's omniscience with his own ignorance, and God's omnipotence with his own impotency. I. He begins with an awakening challenge and demand in general, <reference osisRef="Job.38.2-Job.38.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. II. He proceeds in divers particular instances and proofs of Job's utter inability to contend with God, because of his ignorance and weakness: for, 1. He knew nothing of the founding of the earth, <reference osisRef="Job.38.4-Job.38.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. 2. Nothing of the limiting of the sea, <reference osisRef="Job.38.8-Job.38.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. 3. Nothing of the morning light, <reference osisRef="Job.38.12-Job.38.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. 4. Nothing of the dark recesses of the sea and earth, <reference osisRef="Job.38.16-Job.38.21">ver. 16-21</reference>. 5. Nothing of the springs in the clouds (<reference osisRef="Job.38.22-Job.38.27">ver. 22-27</reference>), nor the secret counsels by which they are directed. 6. He could do nothing towards the production of the rain, or frost, or lightning (<reference osisRef="Job.38.28-Job.38.30 Job.38.34 Job.38.35 Job.38.37 Job.38.38">ver. 28-30, 34, 35, 37, 38</reference>), nothing towards the directing of the stars and their influences (<reference osisRef="Job.38.31-Job.38.33">ver. 31-33</reference>), nothing towards the making of his own soul, <reference osisRef="Job.38.36">ver. 36</reference>. And lastly, he could not provide for the lions and the ravens, <reference osisRef="Job.38.39-Job.38.41">ver. 39-41</reference>. If, in these ordinary works of nature, Job was puzzled, how durst he pretend to dive into the counsels of God's government and to judge of them? In this (as bishop Patrick observes) God takes up the argument begun by Elihu (who came nearest to the truth) and prosecutes it in inimitable words, excelling his, and all other men's, in the loftiness of the style, as much as thunder does a whisper.
entries.05938c445382a1447cc44f9c2f479fe68449b455: <div eID="gen10192" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10191" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God Answers Out of the Whirlwind. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10193" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said, <hi type="super">2</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge? <hi type="super">3</hi> Gird up now thy loins like a man; for I will demand of thee, and answer thou me. <div eID="gen10193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10194" type="x-p"/> Let us observe here, 1. Who speaks—<hi type="italic">The Lord,</hi> Jehovah, not a created angel, but the eternal Word himself, the second person in the blessed Trinity, for it is he by whom the worlds were made, and that was no other than the Son of God. The same speaks here that afterwards spoke from Mount Sinai. Here he begins with the creation of the world, there with the redemption of Israel out of Egypt, and from both is inferred the necessity of our subjection to him. Elihu had said, <hi type="italic">God speaks to men and they do not perceive it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.33.14">ch. xxxiii. 14</reference>); but this they could not but perceive, and yet we have <hi type="italic">a more sure word of prophecy,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.19">2 Pet. i. 19</reference>. 2. When he spoke—<hi type="italic">Then.</hi> When they had all had their saying, and yet had not gained their point, then it was time for God to interpose, whose judgment is according to truth. When we know not who is in the right, and perhaps are doubtful whether we ourselves are, this may satisfy us, That God will determine shortly <hi type="italic">in the valley of decision,</hi> <reference osisRef="Joel.3.14">Joel iii. 14</reference>. Job had silenced his three friends, and yet could not convince them of his integrity in the main. Elihu had silenced Job, and yet could not bring him to acknowledge his mismanagement of this dispute. But now God comes, and does both, convinces Job first of his unadvised speaking and makes him cry, <hi type="italic">Peccavi—I have done wrong;</hi> and, having humbled him, he puts honour upon him, by convincing his three friends that they had done him wrong. These two things God will, sooner or later, do for his people: he will show them their faults, that they may be themselves ashamed of them, and he will show others their righteousness, and bring it forth as the light, that they may be ashamed of their unjust censures of them. 3. How he spoke—<hi type="italic">Out of the whirlwind,</hi> the rolling and involving cloud, which Elihu took notice of, <reference osisRef="Job.37.1-Job.37.2">ch. xxxvii. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.37.9">9</reference>. A whirlwind prefaced Ezekiel's vision (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.4">Ezek. i. 4</reference>), and Elijah's, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.11">1 Kings xix. 11</reference>. God is said to have <hi type="italic">his way in the whirlwind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.3">Nah. i. 3</reference>), and, to show that even the stormy wind fulfils his word, here it was made the vehicle of it. This shows what a mighty voice God's is, that is was not lost, but perfectly audible, even in the noise of a whirlwind. Thus God designed to startled Job, and to command his attention. Sometimes God answers his own people in terrible corrections, as out of the whirlwind, but always in righteousness. 4. To whom he spoke: He <hi type="italic">answered Job,</hi> directed his speech to him, to convince him of what was amiss, before he cleared him from the unjust aspersions cast upon him. It is God only that can effectually convince of sin, and those shall so be humbled whom he designs to exalt. Those that desire to hear from God, as Job did, shall certainly hear from him at length. 5. What he said. We may conjecture that Elihu, or some other of the auditory, wrote down <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> what was delivered out of the whirlwind, for we find (<reference osisRef="Rev.10.4">Rev. x. 4</reference>) that, when the thunders uttered their voices, John was prepared to write. Or, if it was not written then, yet, the penman of the book being inspired by the Holy Ghost, we are sure that we have here a very true and exact report of what was said. <hi type="italic">The Spirit</hi> (says Christ) <hi type="italic">shall bring to your remembrance,</hi> as he did here, <hi type="italic">what I have said to you.</hi> The preface is very searching. (1.) God charges him with ignorance and presumption in what he had said (<reference osisRef="Job.38.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Who is this</hi> that talks at this rate? Is it Job? What! a man? That weak, foolish, despicable, creature—shall he pretend to prescribe to me what I must do or to quarrel with me for what I have done? Is it Job? What! my servant Job, a perfect and an upright man? Can he so far forget himself, and act unlike himself? Who, where, is he <hi type="italic">that darkens counsel thus by words without knowledge?</hi> Let him show his face if he dare, and stand to what he has said." Note, Darkening the counsels of God's wisdom with our folly is a great affront and provocation to God. Concerning God's counsels we must own that we are without knowledge. They are a deep which we cannot fathom; we are quite out of our element, out of our aim, when we pretend to account for them. Yet we are too apt to talk of them as if we understood them, with a great deal of niceness and boldness; but, alas! we do but darken them, instead of explaining them. We confound and perplex ourselves and one another when we dispute of the order of God's decrees, and the designs, and reasons, and methods, of his operations of providence and grace. A humble faith and sincere obedience shall see further and better into the secret of the Lord than all the philosophy of the schools, and the searches of science, so called. This first word which God spoke is the more observable because Job, in his repentance, fastens upon it as that which silenced and humbled him, <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">ch. xlii. 3</reference>. This he repeated and echoed as the arrow that stuck fast in him: "I am the fool that has darkened counsel." There was some colour to have turned it upon <hi type="italic">Elihu,</hi> as if God meant <hi type="italic">him,</hi> for he spoke last, and was speaking when the whirlwind began; but Job applied it to himself, as it becomes us to do when faithful reproofs are given, and not (as most do) to billet them upon other people. (2.) He challenges him to give such proofs of his knowledge as would serve to justify his enquiries into the divine counsels (<reference osisRef="Job.38.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Gird up now thy loins like a</hi> stout <hi type="italic">man;</hi> prepare thyself for the encounter; <hi type="italic">I will demand of thee,</hi> will put some questions to thee, <hi type="italic">and answer me</hi> if thou canst, before I answer thine." Those that go about to call God to an account must expect to be catechised and called to an account themselves, that they may be made sensible of their ignorance and arrogance. God here puts Job in mind of what he had said, <reference osisRef="Job.13.22">ch. xiii. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">Call thou, and I will answer.</hi> "Now make thy words good."
entries.709769eab1b70a9d1770844dbddcc8efb8309aec: <div eID="gen10194" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Creation of the World. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10195" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding. <hi type="super">5</hi> Who hath laid the measures thereof, if thou knowest? or who hath stretched the line upon it? <hi type="super">6</hi> Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? or who laid the corner stone thereof; <hi type="super">7</hi> When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy? <hi type="super">8</hi> Or <hi type="italic">who</hi> shut up the sea with doors, when it brake forth, <hi type="italic">as if</hi> it had issued out of the womb? <hi type="super">9</hi> When I made the cloud the garment thereof, and thick darkness a swaddlingband for it, <hi type="super">10</hi> And brake up for it my decreed <hi type="italic">place,</hi> and set bars and doors, <hi type="super">11</hi> And said, Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed? <div eID="gen10195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10196" type="x-p"/> For the humbling of Job, God here shows him his ignorance even concerning the earth and the sea. Though so near, though so bulky, yet he could give no account of their origination, much less of heaven above or hell beneath, which are at such a distance, or of the several parts of matter which are so minute, and then, least of all, of the divine counsels. <div eID="gen10196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10197" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning the founding of the earth. "If he have such a mighty insight, as he pretends to have, into the counsels of God, let him give some account of the earth he goes upon, which is given to the children of men." <div eID="gen10197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10198" type="x-p"/> 1. Let him tell where he was when this lower world was made, and whether he was advising of assisting in that wonderful work (<reference osisRef="Job.38.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?</hi> Thy pretensions are high; canst thou pretend to his? Wast thou present when the world was made?" See here, (1.) The greatness and glory of God: <hi type="italic">I laid the foundations of the earth.</hi> This proves him to be the only living and true God, and a God of power (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.21">Isa. xl. 21, Jer. x. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.11-Jer.10.12">12</reference>), and encourages us to trust in him at all times, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.13">Isa. li. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.16">16</reference>. (2.) The meanness and contemptibleness of man: "<hi type="italic">Where wast thou</hi> then? Thou that hast made such a figure among the children of the east, and settest up for an oracle, and a judge of the divine counsels, where was thou when the foundations of the earth were laid?" So far were we from having any hand in the creation of the world, which might entitle us to a dominion in it, or so much as being witnesses of it, by which we might have gained an insight into it, that we were not then in being. The first man was not, much less were we. It is the honour of Christ that he was present when this was done (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.22-Prov.8.31 John.1.1-John.1.2">Prov. viii. 22, &c., John i. 1, 2</reference>); but <hi type="italic">we are of yesterday and know nothing.</hi> Let us not therefore find fault with the works of God, nor prescribe to him. He did not consult us in making the world, and yet it is well made; why should we expect then that he should take his measures from us in governing it? <div eID="gen10198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10199" type="x-p"/> 2. Let him describe how this world was made, and give a particular account of the manner in which this strong and stately edifice was formed and erected: "<hi type="italic">Declare, if thou hast</hi> so much <hi type="italic">understanding</hi> as thou fanciest thyself to have, what were the advances of that work." Those that pretend to have understanding above others ought to give proof of it. Show me thy faith by thy works, thy knowledge by thy words. Let Job declare it if he can, (1.) How the world came to be so finely framed, with so much exactness, and such an admirable symmetry and proportion of all the parts of it (<reference osisRef="Job.38.5">v. 5</reference>): "Stand forth, and <hi type="italic">tell who laid the measures thereof</hi> and <hi type="italic">stretched out the line upon it.</hi>" Wast thou the architect that formed the model and then drew the dimensions by rule according to it? The vast bulk of the earth is moulded as regularly as if it had been done by line and measure; but who can describe how it was cast into this figure? Who can determine its circumference and diameter, and all the lines that are drawn on the terrestrial globe? It is to this day a dispute whether the earth stands still or turns round; how then can we determine by what measures it was first formed? (2.) How it came to be so firmly fixed. Though it is hung upon nothing, yet it is established, that it cannot be moved; but who can tell <hi type="italic">upon what the foundations of it are fastened,</hi> that it may not sink with its own weight, or <hi type="italic">who laid the corner-stone thereof,</hi> that the parts of it may not fall asunder? <reference osisRef="Job.38.6">v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">What God does, it shall be for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Eccl. iii. 14</reference>); and therefore, as we cannot find fault with God's work, so we need not be in fear concerning it; it will last, and answer the end, the works of his providence as well as the work of creation; the measures of neither can never be broken; and the work of redemption is no less firm, of which Christ himself is both the foundation and the corner-stone. The church stands as fast as the earth. <div eID="gen10199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10200" type="x-p"/> 3. Let him repeat, if he can, the songs of praise which were sung at that solemnity (<reference osisRef="Job.38.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">when the morning-stars sang together,</hi> the blessed angels (the first-born of the Father of light), who, in the morning of time, shone as brightly as the morning star, going immediately before the light which God commanded to shine out of darkness upon the seeds of this lower world, the earth, which was without form and void. They were <hi type="italic">the sons of God,</hi> who <hi type="italic">shouted for joy</hi> when they saw the foundations of the earth laid, because, though it was not made for them, but for the children of men, and though it would increase their work and service, yet they knew that the eternal Wisdom and Word, whom they were to worship (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">Heb. i. 6</reference>), would <hi type="italic">rejoice in the habitable parts of the earth,</hi> and that much of his <hi type="italic">delight would be in the sons of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.31">Prov. viii. 31</reference>. The angels are called <hi type="italic">the sons of God</hi> because they bear much of his image, are with him in his house above, and serve him as a son does his father. Now observe here, (1.) The glory of God, as the Creator of the world, is to be celebrated with joy and triumph by all his reasonable creatures; for they are qualified and appointed to be the collectors of his praises from the inferior creatures, who can praise him merely as objects that exemplify his workmanship. (2.) The work of angels is to praise God. The more we abound in holy, humble, thankful, joyful praise, the more we do the will of God as they do it; and, whereas we are so barren and defective in praising God, it is a comfort to think that they are doing it in a better manner. (3.) They were unanimous in singing God's praises; they sang together with one accord, and there was no jar in their harmony. The sweetest concerts are in praising God. (4.) They all did it, even those who afterwards fell and left their first estate. Even those who have praised God may, by the deceitful power of sin, be brought to blaspheme him, and yet God will be eternally praised. <div eID="gen10200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10201" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning the limiting of the sea to the place appointed for it, <reference osisRef="Job.38.8">v. 8</reference>, &c. This refers to the third day's work, when God said (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.9">Gen. i. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and it was so.</hi> 1. Out of the great deep or chaos, in which earth and water were intermixed, in obedience to the divine command the waters <hi type="italic">broke forth like a child out of the</hi> teeming <hi type="italic">womb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.8">v. 8</reference>. Then the waters that had covered the deep, and stood above the mountains, retired with precipitation. At <hi type="italic">God's rebuke they fled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.6-Ps.104.7">Ps. civ. 6, 7</reference>. 2. This newborn babe is clothed and swaddled, <reference osisRef="Job.38.9">v. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">The cloud</hi> is made <hi type="italic">the garment thereof,</hi> with which it is covered, and <hi type="italic">thick darkness</hi> (that is, shores vastly remote and distant from one another and quite in the dark one to another) <hi type="italic">is a swaddling-band for it.</hi> See with what ease the great God manages the raging sea; notwithstanding the violence of its tides, and the strength of its billows, he manages it as the nurse does the child in swaddling clothes. It is not said, He made <hi type="italic">rocks and mountains</hi> its swaddling bands, but <hi type="italic">clouds and darkness,</hi> something that we are not aware of and should think least likely for such a purpose. 3. There is a cradle too provided for this babe: <hi type="italic">I broke up for it my decreed place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.10">v. 10</reference>. Valleys were sunk for it in the earth, capacious enough to receive it, and there it is laid to sleep; and, if it be sometimes tossed with winds, that (as bishop Patrick observes) is but the rocking of the cradle, which makes it sleep the faster. As for the sea, so for every one of us, there is a decreed place; for he that determined the times before appointed determined also the bounds of our habitation. 4. This babe being made unruly and dangerous by the sin of man, which was the original of all unquietness and danger in this lower world, there is also a prison provided for it; <hi type="italic">bars and doors are set,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.10">v. 10</reference>. And it is said to it, by way of check to its insolence, <hi type="italic">Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further.</hi> The sea is God's for he made it, he restrains it; he says to it, <hi type="italic">Here shall thy proud waves be stayed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.11">v. 11</reference>. This may be considered as an act of God's power over the sea. Though it is so vast a body, and though its motion is sometimes extremely violent, yet God has it under check. Its waves rise no higher, its tides roll no further, than God permits; and this is mentioned as a reason why we should stand in awe of God (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.22">Jer. v. 22</reference>), and yet why we should encourage ourselves in him, for he that stops the noise of the sea, even the noise of her waves, can, when he pleases, still the tumult of the people, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.7">Ps. lxv. 7</reference>. It is also to be looked upon as an act of God's mercy to the world of mankind and an instance of his patience towards that provoking grace. Though he could easily cover the earth again with the waters of the sea (and, methinks, every flowing tide twice a day threatens us, and shows what the sea could do, and would do, if God would give it leave), yet he restrains them, being not willing that any should perish, and having <hi type="italic">reserved the world that now is unto fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.7">2 Pet. iii. 7</reference>.
entries.956383765bc71cf7ed9e0a3d8ea8b53ed38fc0d2: <div eID="gen10201" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Works of God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10202" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Hast thou commanded the morning since thy days; <hi type="italic">and</hi> caused the dayspring to know his place; <hi type="super">13</hi> That it might take hold of the ends of the earth, that the wicked might be shaken out of it? <hi type="super">14</hi> It is turned as clay <hi type="italic">to</hi> the seal; and they stand as a garment. <hi type="super">15</hi> And from the wicked their light is withholden, and the high arm shall be broken. 16 Hast thou entered into the springs of the sea? or hast thou walked in the search of the depth? <hi type="super">17</hi> Have the gates of death been opened unto thee? or hast thou seen the doors of the shadow of death? <hi type="super">18</hi> Hast thou perceived the breadth of the earth? declare if thou knowest it all. <hi type="super">19</hi> Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the way <hi type="italic">where</hi> light dwelleth? and <hi type="italic">as for</hi> darkness, where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the place thereof, <hi type="super">20</hi> That thou shouldest take it to the bound thereof, and that thou shouldest know the paths <hi type="italic">to</hi> the house thereof? <hi type="super">21</hi> Knowest thou <hi type="italic">it,</hi> because thou wast then born? or <hi type="italic">because</hi> the number of thy days <hi type="italic">is</hi> great? <hi type="super">22</hi> Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail, <hi type="super">23</hi> Which I have reserved against the time of trouble, against the day of battle and war? <hi type="super">24</hi> By what way is the light parted, <hi type="italic">which</hi> scattereth the east wind upon the earth? <div eID="gen10202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10203" type="x-p"/> The Lord here proceeds to ask Job many puzzling questions, to convince him of his ignorance, and so to shame him for his folly in prescribing to God. If we will but try ourselves with such interrogatories as these, we shall soon be brought to own that what we know is nothing in comparison with what we know not. Job is here challenged to give an account of six things:— <div eID="gen10203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10204" type="x-p"/> I. Of the springs of the morning, the day-spring from on high, <reference osisRef="Job.38.12-Job.38.15">v. 12-15</reference>. As there is no visible being of which we may be more firmly assured that it is, so there is none which we are more puzzled in describing, nor more doubtful in determining what it is, than the light. We welcome the morning, and are glad of the day-spring; but, 1. It is not commanded since our days, but what it is it was long before we were born, so that it was neither made by us nor designed primarily for us, but we take it as we find it and as the many generations had it that went before us. The day-spring knew its place before we knew ours, for we are but of yesterday. 2. It was not we, it was not any man that commanded the morning-light at first, or appointed the place of its springing up and shining forth, or the time of it. The constant and regular succession of day and night was no contrivance of ours; it is the glory of God that it shows, and his handy work, not ours, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.2">Ps. xix. 1, 2</reference>. 3. It is quite out of our power to alter this course: "<hi type="italic">Hast thou countermanded the morning since thy days?</hi> Hast thou at any time raised the morning light sooner than its appointed time, to serve thy purpose when thou hast waited for the morning, or ordered the day-spring for thy convenience to any other place than its own? No, never. Why then wilt thou pretend to direct the divine counsels, or expect to have the methods of Providence altered in favour of thee?" We may as soon break the covenant of the day and of the night as any part of God's covenant with his people, and particularly this, <hi type="italic">I will chasten them with the rod of men.</hi> 4. It is God that has appointed the day-spring to visit the earth, and diffuses the morning light through the air, which receives it as readily as the clay does the seal (<reference osisRef="Job.38.14">v. 14</reference>), immediately admitting the impressions of it, so as of a sudden to be all over enlightened by it, as the seal stamps its image on the wax; <hi type="italic">and they stand as a garment,</hi> or as if they were clothed with a garment. The earth puts on a new face every morning, and dresses itself as we do, puts on light as a garment, and is then to be seen. 5. This is made a terror to evil-doers. Nothing is more comfortable to mankind than the light of the morning; it is pleasant to the eyes, it is serviceable to life and the business of it, and the favour of it is universally extended, for <hi type="italic">it takes hold of the ends of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.13">v. 13</reference>), and we should dwell, in our hymns to the light, on its advantages to the earth. But God here observes how unwelcome it is to those that do evil, and therefore hate the light. God makes the light a minister of his justice as well as of his mercy. It is designed <hi type="italic">to shake the wicked out of the earth,</hi> and for that purpose <hi type="italic">it takes hold of the ends of it,</hi> as we take hold of the ends of a garment to shake the dust and moths out of it. Job had observed what a terror the morning light is to criminals, because it discovers them (<reference osisRef="Job.24.13-Job.24.16">ch. xxiv. 13</reference>, &c.), and God here seconds the observation, and asks him whether the world was indebted to him for that kindness? No, the great Judge of the world sends forth the beams of the morning light as his messengers to detect criminals, that they may not only be defeated in their purposes and put to shame, but that they may be brought to condign punishment (<reference osisRef="Job.38.15">v. 15</reference>), that their light may be <hi type="italic">withholden</hi> from them (that is, that they may lose their comfort, their confidence, their liberties, their lives) and that their <hi type="italic">high arm,</hi> which they have lifted up against God and man, may be <hi type="italic">broken,</hi> and they deprived of their power to do mischief. Whether what is here said of the morning light was designed to represent, as in a figure, the light of the gospel of Christ, and to give a type of it, I will not say; but I am sure it may serve to put us in mind of the encomiums given to the gospel just at the rising of its morning-star by Zecharias in his <hi type="italic">Benedictus</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.78">Luke i. 78</reference>, By the <hi type="italic">tender mercy of our God the day-spring from on high has visited us, to give light to those that sit in darkness,</hi> whose hearts are turned to it <hi type="italic">as clay to the seal,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6</reference>), and by the virgin Mary in her <hi type="italic">Magnificat</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.51">Luke i. 51</reference>), showing that God, in his gospel, has <hi type="italic">shown strength with his arm, scattered the proud, and put down the mighty,</hi> by that light by which he designed to shake the wicked, to shake wickedness itself out of the earth, and break its high arm. <div eID="gen10204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10205" type="x-p"/> II. Of the springs of the sea (<reference osisRef="Job.38.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hast thou entered into</hi> them, or <hi type="italic">hast thou walked in the search of the depth?</hi> Knowest thou what lies in the bottom of the sea, the treasures there hidden in the sands? Or canst thou give an account of the rise and original of the waters of the sea? Vapours are continually exhaled out of the sea. Dost thou know how the recruits are raised by which it is continually supplied? Rivers are constantly poured into the sea. Dost thou know how they are continually discharged, so as not to overflow the earth? Art thou acquainted with the secret subterraneous passages by which the waters circulate?" God's way in the government of the world is said to be <hi type="italic">in the sea,</hi> and <hi type="italic">in the great waters</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">Ps. lxxvii. 19</reference>), intimating that it is hidden from us and not to be pried into by us. <div eID="gen10205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10206" type="x-p"/> III. Of the gates of death: <hi type="italic">Have</hi> these <hi type="italic">been open to thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.16">v. 16</reference>. Death is a grand secret. 1. We know not beforehand when, and how, and by what means, we or others shall be brought to death, by what road we must go the way whence we shall not return, what disease or what disaster will be the door to let us into the house appointed for all living. <hi type="italic">Man knows not his time.</hi> 2. We cannot describe what death is, how the knot is untied between body and soul, nor how the <hi type="italic">spirit of a man goes upward</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.21">Eccl. iii. 21</reference>), to be we know not what and live we know not how, as Mr. Norris expresses; with what dreadful curiosity (says he) does the soul launch out into the vast ocean of eternity and resign to an untried abyss! Let us make it sure that the gates of heaven shall be opened to us on the other side death, and then we need not fear the opening of the gates of death, though it is a way we are to go but once. 3. We have no correspondence at all with separate souls, nor any acquaintance with their state. It is an unknown undiscovered region to which they are removed; we can neither hear from them nor send to them. While we are here, in a world of sense, we speak of the world of spirits as blind men do of colours, and when we remove thither we shall be amazed to find how much we are mistaken. <div eID="gen10206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10207" type="x-p"/> IV. Of the breadth of the earth (<reference osisRef="Job.38.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hast thou perceived</hi> that? The knowledge of this might seem most level to him and within his reach; yet he is challenged to declare this if he can. We have our residence on the earth, God has given it to the children of men. But who ever surveyed it, or could give an account of the number of its acres? It is but a point to the universe? yet, small as it is, we cannot be exact in declaring the dimensions of it. Job had never sailed round the world, nor any before him; so little did men know the breadth of the earth that it was but a few ages ago that the vast continent of America was discovered, which had, time out of mind, lain hidden. The divine perfection is longer than the earth and broader than the sea; it is therefore presumption for us, who perceive not the breadth of the earth, to dive into the depth of God's counsels. <div eID="gen10207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10208" type="x-p"/> V. Of the place and way of light and darkness. Of the day-spring he had spoken before (<reference osisRef="Job.38.12">v. 12</reference>) and he returns to speak of it again (<reference osisRef="Job.38.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Where is the way where light dwells?</hi> And again (<reference osisRef="Job.38.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">By what way is the light parted?</hi> He challenges him to describe, 1. How the light and darkness were at first made. When God, in the beginning, first spread darkness upon the face of the deep, and afterwards commanded the light to shine out of darkness, by that mighty word, <hi type="italic">Let there be light,</hi> was Job a witness to the order, to the operation? can he tell where the fountains of light and darkness are, and where those mighty princes keep their courts distance, while in one world they rule alternately? Though we long ever so much either for the shining forth of the morning or the shadows of the evening, we know not whither to send, or go, to fetch them, nor can tell <hi type="italic">the paths to the house thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.20">v. 20</reference>. We were not then born, nor is the number of our days so great that we can describe the birth of that first-born of the visible creation, <reference osisRef="Job.38.21">v. 21</reference>. Shall we then undertake to discourse of God's counsels, which were from eternity, or to find out the paths to the house thereof, to solicit for the alteration of them? God glories in it that he forms the light and creates the darkness; and if we must take those as we find them, take those as they come, and quarrel with neither, but make the best of both, then we must, in like manner, accommodate ourselves to the peace and the evil which God likewise created. <reference osisRef="Isa.45.7">Isa. xlv. 7</reference>. 2. How they still keep their turns interchangeably. It is God that <hi type="italic">makes the outgoings of the morning and of the evening to rejoice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.8">Ps. lxv. 8</reference>); for it is his order, and no order of ours, that is executed by the outgoings of the morning light and the darkness of the night. We cannot so much as tell whence they come nor whither they go (<reference osisRef="Job.38.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">By what way is the light parted</hi> in the morning, when, in an instant, it shoots itself into all the parts of the air above the horizon, as if the morning light flew upon the wings of an east wind, so swiftly, so strongly, is it carried, scattering the darkness of the night, as the east wind does the clouds? Hence we read of the <hi type="italic">wings of the morning</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.9">Ps. cxxxix. 9</reference>), on which the light is conveyed <hi type="italic">to the uttermost parts of the sea,</hi> and <hi type="italic">scattered like an east wind upon the earth.</hi> It is a marvellous change that passes over us every morning by the return of the light and every evening by the return of the darkness; but we expect them, and so they are no surprise nor uneasiness to us. If we would, in like manner, reckon upon changes in our outward condition, we should neither in the brightest noon expect perpetual day nor in the darkest midnight despair of the return of the morning. God has set the one over against the other, like the day and night; and so must we, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Eccl. vii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen10208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10209" type="x-p"/> VI. Of the <hi type="italic">treasures of the snow and hail</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.22-Job.38.23">v. 22, 23</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hast thou entered</hi> into these and taken a view of them?" In the clouds the snow and hail are generated, and thence they come in such abundance that one would think there were treasures of them laid up in store there, whereas indeed they are produced <hi type="italic">extempore</hi>—<hi type="italic">suddenly,</hi> as I may say, and <hi type="italic">pro re nata</hi>—<hi type="italic">for the occasion.</hi> Sometimes they come so opportunely, to serve the purposes of Providence, in God's fighting for his people and against his and their enemies, that one would think they were laid up as magazines, or stores of arms, ammunition, and provisions, against the time of trouble, <hi type="italic">the day of battle and war,</hi> when God will either contend with the world in general (as in the deluge, when the windows of heaven were opened, and the waters fetched out of these treasures to drown a wicked world, that waged war with Heaven) or with some particular persons or parties, as when God out of these treasures fetched great hail-stones wherewith to fight against the Canaanites, <reference osisRef="Josh.10.11">Josh. x. 11</reference>. See what folly it is to strive against God, who is thus prepared for battle and war, and how much it is our interest to make our peace with him and to keep ourselves in his love. God can fight as effectually with snow and hail, if he please, as with thunder and lightning or the sword of an angel!
entries.39d90182a460b7391f3ac37bf6450294a21ed67b: <div eID="gen10209" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Sovereign Dominion and Goodness. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10210" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder; 26 To cause it to rain on the earth, <hi type="italic">where</hi> no man <hi type="italic">is; on</hi> the wilderness, wherein <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no man; 27 To satisfy the desolate and waste <hi type="italic">ground;</hi> and to cause the bud of the tender herb to spring forth? <hi type="super">28</hi> Hath the rain a father? or who hath begotten the drops of dew? <hi type="super">29</hi> Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it? <hi type="super">30</hi> The waters are hid as <hi type="italic">with</hi> a stone, and the face of the deep is frozen. <hi type="super">31</hi> Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion? 32 Canst thou bring forth Mazzaroth in his season? or canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons? <hi type="super">33</hi> Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? canst thou set the dominion thereof in the earth? <hi type="super">34</hi> Canst thou lift up thy voice to the clouds, that abundance of waters may cover thee? <hi type="super">35</hi> Canst thou send lightnings, that they may go, and say unto thee, Here we <hi type="italic">are?</hi> <hi type="super">36</hi> Who hath put wisdom in the inward parts? or who hath given understanding to the heart? <hi type="super">37</hi> Who can number the clouds in wisdom? or who can stay the bottles of heaven, <hi type="super">38</hi> When the dust groweth into hardness, and the clods cleave fast together? <hi type="super">39</hi> Wilt thou hunt the prey for the lion? or fill the appetite of the young lions, <hi type="super">40</hi> When they couch in <hi type="italic">their</hi> dens, <hi type="italic">and</hi> abide in the covert to lie in wait? 41 Who provideth for the raven his food? when his young ones cry unto God, they wander for lack of meat. <div eID="gen10210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10211" type="x-p"/> Hitherto God had put such questions to Job as were proper to convince him of his ignorance and short-sightedness. Now he comes, in the same manner, to show his impotency and weakness. As it is but little that he knows, and therefore he ought not to arraign the divine counsels, so it is but little that he can do, and therefore he ought not to oppose the proceedings of Providence. Let him consider what great things God does, and try whether he can do the like, or whether he thinks himself an equal match for him. <div eID="gen10211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10212" type="x-p"/> I. God has thunder, and lightning, and rain, and frost, at command, but Job has not, and therefore let him not dare to compare himself with God, or to contend with him. Nothing is more uncertain than what weather it shall be, nor more out of our reach to appoint; it shall be what weather pleases God, not what pleases us, unless, as becomes us, whatever pleases God pleases us. Concerning this observe here, <div eID="gen10212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10213" type="x-p"/> 1. How great God is. <div eID="gen10213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10214" type="x-p"/> (1.) He has a sovereign dominion over the waters, has appointed them their course, even then when they seem to overflow and to be from under his check, <reference osisRef="Job.38.25">v. 25</reference>. He has <hi type="italic">divided a water-course,</hi> directs the rain where to fall, even when the shower is most violent, with as much certainty as if it were conveyed by canals or conduit-pipes. Thus the hearts of kings are said to be <hi type="italic">in God's hand;</hi> and as the rains, those rivers of God, he turns them whithersoever he will. Every drop goes as it is directed. God has <hi type="italic">sworn that the waters of Noah shall no more return to cover the earth;</hi> and we see that he is able to make good what he has promised, for he has the rain in a water-course. <div eID="gen10214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10215" type="x-p"/> (2.) He has dominion over the lightning and the thunder, which go not at random, but in the way that he directs them. They are mentioned here because he <hi type="italic">prepares the lightnings for the rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Ps. cxxxv. 7</reference>. Let not those that fear God be afraid of the lightning or the thunder, for they are not blind bullets, but go the way that God himself, who means no hurt to them, directs. <div eID="gen10215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10216" type="x-p"/> (3.) In directing the course of the rain he does not neglect the wilderness, the desert land (<reference osisRef="Job.38.26-Job.38.27">v. 26, 27</reference>), <hi type="italic">where no man is.</hi> [1.] Where there is no man to be employed in taking care of the productions. God's providence reaches further than man's industry. If he had not more kindness for many of the inferior creatures than man has, it would go ill with them. God can make the earth fruitful without any art or pains of ours, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.5-Gen.2.6">Gen. ii. 5, 6</reference>. When <hi type="italic">there was not a man to till the ground,</hi> yet there went up a mist and watered it. But we cannot make it fruitful without God; it is he that gives the increase. [2.] Where there is no man to be provided for nor to take the benefit of the fruits that are produced. Though God does with very peculiar favour visit and regard man, yet he does not overlook the inferior creatures, but causes <hi type="italic">the bud of the tender herb to spring forth for food for all flesh,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">for the service of man.</hi> Even the wild asses shall have their thirst quenched, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.11">Ps. civ. 11</reference>. God has enough for all, and wonderfully provides even for those creatures that man neither has service from nor makes provision for. <div eID="gen10216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10217" type="x-p"/> (4.) He is, in a sense, <hi type="italic">the Father of the rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.28">v. 28</reference>. It has no other father. He produces it by his power; he governs and directs it, and makes what use he pleases of it. Even the small drops of the dew he distils upon the earth, as the God of nature; and, as the God of grace, he rains righteousness upon us and is himself as the dew unto Israel. See <reference osisRef="Hos.14.5">Hos. xiv. 5, 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mic. v. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen10217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10218" type="x-p"/> (5.) The ice and the frost, by which the waters are congealed and the earth incrustrated, are produced by his providence, <reference osisRef="Job.38.29-Job.38.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. These are very common things, which lessens the strangeness of them. But, considering what a vast change is made by them in a very little time, how the waters are hid as with a stone, as with a grave-stone, laid upon them (so thick, so strong, is the ice that covers them), and the face even of the deep is sometimes frozen, we may well ask, "<hi type="italic">Out of whose womb came the ice?</hi> What created power could produce such a wonderful work?" No power but that of the Creator himself. Frost and snow come from him, and therefore should lead our thoughts and meditations to him who does such great things, past finding out. And we shall the more easily bear the inconveniences of winter-weather if we learn to make this good use of it. <div eID="gen10218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10219" type="x-p"/> 2. How weak man is. Can he do such things as these? Could Job? No, <reference osisRef="Job.38.34-Job.38.35">v. 34, 35</reference>. (1.) He cannot command one shower of rain for the relief of himself or his friends: "<hi type="italic">Canst thou lift up thy voice to the clouds,</hi> those bottles of heaven, <hi type="italic">that abundance of waters may cover thee,</hi> to water thy fields when they are dry and parched?" If we lift up our voice to God, to pray for rain, we may have it (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.1">Zech. x. 1</reference>); but if we lift up our voice to the clouds, to demand it, they will soon tell us they are not at our beck, and we shall go without it, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.22">Jer. xiv. 22</reference>. The heavens will not hear the earth unless God hear them, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.21">Hos. ii. 21</reference>. See what poor, indigent, depending creatures we are; we cannot do without rain, nor can we have it when we will. (2.) He cannot commission one flash of lightning, if he had a mind to make use of it for the terror of his enemies (<reference osisRef="Job.38.35">v. 35</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Canst thou send lightnings, that they may go</hi> on thy errand, and do the execution thou desirest? Will they come at thy call, and say unto thee, <hi type="italic">Here we are?</hi>" No, the ministers of God's wrath will not be ministers of ours. Why should they, since the <hi type="italic">wrath of man works not the righteousness of God?</hi> See <reference osisRef="Luke.9.55">Luke ix. 55</reference>. <div eID="gen10219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10220" type="x-p"/> II. God has the stars of heaven under his command and cognizance, but we have them not under ours. Our meditations are now to rise higher, far above the clouds, to the glorious lights above. God mentions particularly, not the planets, which move in lower orbs, but the fixed stars, which are much higher. It is supposed that they have an influence upon this earth, notwithstanding their vast distance, not upon the minds of men or the events of providence (men's fate is not determined by their stars), but upon the ordinary course of nature; they are set for signs and seasons, for days and years, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.14">Gen. i. 14</reference>. And if the stars have such a dominion over this earth (<reference osisRef="Job.38.33">v. 33</reference>), though they have their place in the heavens and are but mere matter, much more has he who is their Maker and ours, and who is an Eternal Mind. Now see how weak we are. 1. We cannot alter the influences of the stars (<reference osisRef="Job.38.31">v. 31</reference>), not theirs that are instrumental to produce the pleasures of the spring: <hi type="italic">Canst thou loose the bands of Orion?</hi>—that magnificent constellation which makes so great a figure (none greater), and dispenses rough and unpleasing influences, which we cannot control nor repel. Both summer and winter will have their course. God can change them when he pleases, can make the spring cold, and so bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, and the winter warm, and so loose the bands of Orion; but we cannot. 2. It is not in our power to order the motions of the stars, nor are we entrusted with the guidance of them. God, who <hi type="italic">calls the stars by their names</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.4">Ps. cxlvii. 4</reference>), calls them forth in their respective seasons, appointing them the time of their rising and setting. But this is not our province; we cannot <hi type="italic">bring forth Mazzaroth</hi>—the stars in the southern signs, nor <hi type="italic">guide Arcturus</hi>—those in the northern, <reference osisRef="Job.38.32">v. 32</reference>. God can bring forth the stars to battle (as he did when in their courses they fought against Sisera) and guide them in the attacks they are ordered to make; but man cannot do so. 3. We are not only unconcerned in the government of the stars (the government they are under, and the government they are entrusted with, for they both rule and are ruled), but utterly unacquainted with it; we <hi type="italic">know not the ordinances of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.33">v. 33</reference>. So far are we from being able to change them that we can give no account of them; they are a secret to us. Shall we then pretend to know God's counsels, and the reasons of them? If it were left to us to set the dominion of the stars upon the earth, we should soon be at a loss. Shall we then teach God how to govern the world? <div eID="gen10220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10221" type="x-p"/> III. God is the author and giver, the father and fountain, of all wisdom and understanding, <reference osisRef="Job.38.36">v. 36</reference>. The souls of men are nobler and more excellent beings than the stars of heaven themselves, and shine more brightly. The powers and faculties of reason with which man is endued, and the wonderful performances of thought, bring him into some alliance to the blessed angels; and whence comes this light, but from the Father of lights? <hi type="italic">Who</hi> else <hi type="italic">has put wisdom into the inner parts</hi> of man, and <hi type="italic">given understanding to the heart?</hi> 1. The rational soul itself, and its capacities, come from him as the God of nature; for he forms the spirit of man within him. We did not make our own souls, nor can we describe how they act, nor how they are united to our bodies. He only that made them knows them, and knows how to manage them. He fashioneth men's hearts alike in some things, and yet unlike in others. 2. True wisdom, with its furniture and improvement, comes from him as the God of grace and the Father of every good and perfect gift. Shall we pretend to be wiser than God, when we have all our wisdom from him? Nay, shall we pretend to be wise above our sphere, and beyond the limits which he that gave us our understanding sets to it? He designed we should with it serve God and do our duty, but never intended we should with it set up for directors of the stars or the lightning. <div eID="gen10221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10222" type="x-p"/> IV. God has the clouds under his cognizance and government, but so have not we, <reference osisRef="Job.38.37">v. 37</reference>. Can any man, with all his wisdom, undertake to <hi type="italic">number the clouds,</hi> or (as it may be read) to <hi type="italic">declare and describe the nature of them?</hi> Though they are near us, in our own atmosphere, yet we know little more of them than of the stars which are at so great a distance. And when the clouds have poured down rain in abundance, so that <hi type="italic">the dust grows into</hi> solid mire and <hi type="italic">the clods cleave fast together</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.38">v. 38</reference>), <hi type="italic">who can stay the bottles of heaven?</hi> Who can stop them, that it may not always rain? The power and goodness of God are herein to be acknowledged, that he gives the earth rain enough, but does not surfeit it, softens it, but does not drown it, makes it fit for the plough, but not unfit for the seed. As we cannot command a shower of rain, so we cannot command a fair day, without God; so necessary, so constant, is our dependence upon him. <div eID="gen10222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10223" type="x-p"/> V. God provides food for the inferior creatures, and it is by his providence, not by any care or pains of ours, that they are fed. The following chapter is wholly taken up with the instances of God's power and goodness about animals, and therefore some transfer to it the last three verses of this chapter, which speak of the provision made, 1. For the lions, <reference osisRef="Job.38.39-Job.38.40">v. 39, 40</reference>. "Thou dost not pretend that the clouds and stars have any dependence upon thee, for they are above thee; but on the earth thou thinkest thyself paramount; let us try that then: <hi type="italic">Wilt thou hunt the prey for the lion?</hi> Thou valuest thyself upon thy possessions of cattle which thou wast once owner of, the oxen, and asses, and camels, that were fed at thy crib; but wilt thou undertake the maintenance of the lions, and <hi type="italic">the young lions, when they couch in their dens,</hi> waiting for a prey? No, needest not do it, they can shift for themselves without thee: thou canst not do it, for thou hast not wherewithal to satisfy them: thou darest not do it; shouldst thou come to feed them, they would seize upon thee. But I do it." See the all-sufficiency of the divine providence: it has wherewithal to satisfy the desire of every living thing, even the most ravenous. See the bounty of the divine Providence, that, wherever it has given life, it will give livelihood, even to those creatures that are not only not serviceable, but dangerous, to man. And see its sovereignty, that it suffers some creatures to be killed for the support of other creatures. The harmless sheep are torn to pieces, to <hi type="italic">fill the appetite of the young lions,</hi> who yet sometimes are made to lack and suffer hunger, to punish them for their cruelty, while those that fear God want no good thing. 2. For the young ravens, <reference osisRef="Job.38.41">v. 41</reference>. As ravenous beasts, so ravenous birds, are fed by the divine Providence. <hi type="italic">Who</hi> but God <hi type="italic">provides for the raven his food?</hi> Man does not; he takes care only of those creatures that are, or may be, useful to him. But God has a regard to all the works of his hands, even the meanest and least valuable. The ravens' <hi type="italic">young ones</hi> are in a special manner necessitous, and God supplies them, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.9">Ps. cxlvii. 9</reference>. God's feeding the fowls, especially these fowls (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.26">Matt. vi. 26</reference>), is an encouragement to us to trust him for our daily bread. See here, (1.) What distress the young ravens are often in: <hi type="italic">They wander for lack of meat.</hi> The old ones, they say, neglect them, and do not provide for them as other birds do for their young: and indeed those that are ravenous to others are commonly barbarous to their own, and unnatural. (2.) What they are supposed to do in that distress: They <hi type="italic">cry,</hi> for they are noisy clamorous creatures, and this is interpreted as crying to God. It being the cry of nature, it is looked upon as directed to the God of nature. The putting of so favourable a construction as this upon the cries of the young ravens may encourage us in our prayers, though we can but cry, <hi type="italic">Abba, Father.</hi> (3.) What God does for them. Some way or other he provides for them, so that they grow up, and come to maturity. And he that takes this care of the young ravens certainly will not be wanting to his people or theirs. This, being but one instance of many of the divine compassion, may give us occasion to think how much good our God does, every day, beyond what we are aware of.  <chapter eID="Job.38"/> <div eID="gen10223" type="x-p"/>

entries.27a1df4d7ad99f5588668e5cf8141a4d48a5ebb9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5315"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 38</title> <div sID="gen7966" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.38.1-Job.38.41">Job 38:1-41</reference>.<div eID="gen7966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7967" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5315"/>1. Jehovah appears unexpectedly in a whirlwind (already gathering <reference osisRef="Job.37.1">Job 37:1</reference>, 2), the symbol of "judgment" (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.3">Psa 50:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.4">4</reference>, &c.), to which Job had challenged Him. He asks him now to get himself ready for the contest. Can he explain the phenomena of God's natural government? How can he, then, hope to understand the principles of His moral government? God thus confirms Elihu's sentiment, that submission to, not reasonings on, God's ways is man's part. This and the disciplinary design of trial to the godly is the great lesson of this book. He does not solve the difficulty by reference to future retribution: for this was not the immediate question; glimpses of that truth were already given in the fourteenth and nineteenth chapters, the full revelation of it being reserved for Gospel times. Yet even now we need to learn the lesson taught by Elihu and God in Job. <div eID="gen7967" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e6cf1592db287abc28acc1853bf43124965d3f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5316"/><div sID="gen7968" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5316"/><hi type="bold">2. this--</hi>Job.<div eID="gen7968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7969" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">counsel--</hi>impugning My divine wisdom in the providential arrangements of the universe. Such "words" (including those of the friends) rather obscure, than throw light on My ways. God is about to be Job's Vindicator, but must first bring him to a right state of mind for receiving relief. <div eID="gen7969" type="x-p"/>
entries.0bb7acc5abf415eeade8e0f1b9dc03ab79cda9ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5317"/><div sID="gen7970" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5317"/><hi type="bold">3. a man--</hi>hero, ready for battle (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.13">1Co 16:13</reference>), as he had wished (<reference osisRef="Job.9.35">Job 9:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.22">13:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.37">31:37</reference>). The robe, usually worn flowing, was girt up by a girdle when men ran, labored, or fought (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.13">1Pe 1:13</reference>). <div eID="gen7970" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3f39d1b43c811ad3fc61cc115fa95a331fe2e29: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5318"/><div sID="gen7971" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5318"/>4. To understand the cause of things, man should have been present at their origin. The finite creature cannot fathom the infinite wisdom of the Creator (<reference osisRef="Job.28.12">Job 28:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.7">15:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.15.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen7971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7972" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hast--</hi>"knowest."<div eID="gen7972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">understanding--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.4.1">Pr 4:1</reference>). <div eID="gen7973" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e55e7c23a78669a5b2cca67e5962c4d65d2befa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5319"/><div sID="gen7974" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5319"/><hi type="bold">5. measures--</hi>of its proportions. Image from an architect's plans of a building.<div eID="gen7974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">line--</hi>of measurement (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">Is 28:17</reference>). The earth is formed on an all-wise plan. <div eID="gen7975" type="x-p"/>
entries.07deb1cf97f872e38d5acc959ee71ee3abbaf0d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5320"/><div sID="gen7976" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5320"/><hi type="bold">6. foundations--</hi>not "sockets," as Margin.<div eID="gen7976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7977" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fastened--</hi>literally, "made to sink," as a foundation-stone let down till it settles firmly in the clay (<reference osisRef="Job.26.7">Job 26:7</reference>). Gravitation makes and keeps the earth a sphere. <div eID="gen7977" type="x-p"/>
entries.63b574b57e9ab745fae063ea8e42c53bf8732c57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5321"/><div sID="gen7978" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5321"/>7. So at the founding of Zerubbabel's temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.10-Ezra.3.13">Ezr 3:10-13</reference>). So hereafter at the completion of the Church, the temple of the Holy Ghost (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.7">Zec 4:7</reference>); as at its foundation (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.13">Lu 2:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen7978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">morning stars--</hi>especially beautiful. The creation morn is appropriately associated with these, it being the commencement of this world's day. The stars are figuratively said to sing God's praises, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1">Psa 19:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.148.3">148:3</reference>. They are symbols of the angels, bearing the same relation to our earth, as angels do to us. Therefore they answer to "sons of God," or angels, in the parallel. See on <reference osisRef="Job.25.5">Job 25:5</reference>. <div eID="gen7979" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9596edec0b7ee3e67b5b7868dfa87beb56f1269: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5322"/><div sID="gen7980" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5322"/><hi type="bold">8. doors--</hi>floodgates; these when opened caused the flood (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.2">Ge 8:2</reference>); or else, the shores.<div eID="gen7980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7981" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">womb--</hi>of chaos. The bowels of the earth. Image from childbirth (<reference osisRef="Job.38.8">Job 38:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.38.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.2">Eze 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.10">Mi 4:10</reference>). Ocean at its birth was wrapped in clouds as its swaddling bands. <div eID="gen7981" type="x-p"/>
entries.f99d9f3148cb891863fed812838a87e0768d9849: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5323"/><div sID="gen7982" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5323"/><hi type="bold">10. brake up for--</hi>that is, appointed it. Shores are generally broken and abrupt cliffs. The Greek for "shore" means "a broken place." I broke off or measured off for it my limit, that is, the limit which I thought fit (<reference osisRef="Job.26.10">Job 26:10</reference>). <div eID="gen7982" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b469d5e7e318e5ddbe2f7278bc5f62a76be0eae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5324"/><div sID="gen7983" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5324"/><hi type="bold">11. stayed--</hi>Hebrew, "a limit shall be set to." <div eID="gen7983" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ff9601c1fae0f6824a2f000c38c7513af9a188b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5325"/><div sID="gen7984" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5325"/>12-15. Passing from creation to phenomena in the existing inanimate world.<div eID="gen7984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7985" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hast thou--</hi>as God daily does.<div eID="gen7985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7986" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commanded the morning--</hi>to rise.<div eID="gen7986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7987" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">since thy days--</hi>since thou hast come into being.<div eID="gen7987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7988" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his place--</hi>It varies in its place of rising from day to day, and yet it has its place each day according to fixed laws. <div eID="gen7988" type="x-p"/>
entries.b27e8833f57d1e28c3152fa1a438644a06a25f23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5329"/><div sID="gen7997" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5329"/><hi type="bold">16. springs--</hi>fountains beneath the sea (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.4">Psa 95:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.95.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen7997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">search--</hi>Rather, "the inmost recesses"; literally, "that which is only found by searching," the deep caverns of ocean. <div eID="gen7998" type="x-p"/>
entries.21dce2ead71f0b7bd4ba2725ffc5b32d66300721: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5330"/><div sID="gen7999" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5330"/><hi type="bold">17. seen--</hi>The second clause heightens the thought in the first. Man during life does not even "see" the gates of the realm of the dead ("death," <reference osisRef="Job.10.21">Job 10:21</reference>); much less are they "opened" to him. But those are "naked before God" (<reference osisRef="Job.26.6">Job 26:6</reference>). <div eID="gen7999" type="x-p"/>
entries.0864e54a861d6894d3b571c9a3c0027b3a133679: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5331"/><div sID="gen8000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5331"/><hi type="bold">18. Hast thou--</hi>as God doth (<reference osisRef="Job.28.24">Job 28:24</reference>). <div eID="gen8000" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d8d9498e859da1fc9c5b80fbc510ecacbf56694: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5332"/><div sID="gen8001" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5332"/>19-38. The marvels in heaven. "What is the way (to the place wherein) light dwelleth?" The origin of light and darkness. In Ge 1:3-5, 14-18, "light" is created distinct from, and previous to, light-emitting bodies, the luminaries of heaven. <div eID="gen8001" type="x-p"/>
entries.de685c62198e249ac64f622fbf43e5e998858812: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5352"/><div sID="gen8031" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5352"/>39. At <reference osisRef="Job.38.39-Job.39.30">Job 38:39-39:30</reference>, the instincts of animals. Is it thou that givest it the instinct to hunt its prey? (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.21">Psa 104:21</reference>).<div eID="gen8031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appetite--</hi>literally, "life," which depends on the appetite" (<reference osisRef="Job.33.20">Job 33:20</reference>). <div eID="gen8032" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a6ab5ab75e4c6379f02e703c3162aa9a86386d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5353"/><div sID="gen8033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5353"/><hi type="bold">40. lie in wait?--</hi>for their prey (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.9">Psa 10:9</reference>). <div eID="gen8033" type="x-p"/>
entries.be2fd4e3ffc8ed39c3cd8ba028c6fe08e1d7e43c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5354"/><div sID="gen8034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5354"/>41. <reference osisRef="Luke.12.24">Lu 12:24</reference>. entries.fd679e486047adbbb5596096bf8dd8c3788f9ba2: <div eID="gen17844" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17845" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17846" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17846" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17845" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17847" type="x-p"/> The Lord answers Job out of a whirlwind, and challenges him to answer, <reference osisRef="Job.38.1-Job.38.3">Job 38:1-3</reference>. He convinces him of ignorance and weakness, by an enumeration of some of his mighty works; particularly of the creation of the earth, <reference osisRef="Job.38.4-Job.38.7">Job 38:4-7</reference>. The sea and the deeps, <reference osisRef="Job.38.8-Job.38.18">Job 38:8-18</reference>. The light, <reference osisRef="Job.38.19-Job.38.21">Job 38:19-21</reference>. Snow, hail, thunder, lightning, rain, dew, ice, and hoar-frost, <reference osisRef="Job.38.22-Job.38.30">Job 38:22-30</reference>. Different constellations, and the ordinances of heaven influencing the earth, <reference osisRef="Job.38.31-Job.38.33">Job 38:31-33</reference>. Shows his own power and wisdom in the atmosphere, particularly in the thunder, lightnings, and rain, <reference osisRef="Job.38.34-Job.38.38">Job 38:34-38</reference>. His providence in reference to the brute creation, <reference osisRef="Job.38.39-Job.38.41">Job 38:39-41</reference>. <div eID="gen17847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17848" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen17848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17849" type="x-p"/> The Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind - It is not סופה suphah, as in the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="Job.37.9">Job 37:9</reference>; but סורה searah, which signifies something turbulent, tumultuous, or violently agitated; and here may signify what we call a tempest, and was intended to fill Job's mind with solemnity, and an awful sense of the majesty of God. The Chaldee has, a whirlwind of grief, making the whole rather allegorical than real; impressing the scene on Job's imagination.
entries.b1d8cb906fb4bb78334c5eea2a20e0053c068129: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17850" type="x-p"/> Who is this that darkeneth counsel - As if he had said, Who art thou who pretendest to speak on the deep things of God, and the administration of his justice and providence, which thou canst not comprehend; and leavest my counsels and designs the darker for thy explanation?
entries.efe903df002e07b3593eb821dca52055d10e25ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17851" type="x-p"/> Gird up now thy loins - I will not confound thee with my terrors; dismiss all fearful apprehensions from thy mind; now act like a man, כגבר kegeber, like a hero: stand and vindicate thyself. For I will demand of thee - I will ask thee a series of questions more easy of solution than those which thou hast affected to discuss already; and then thou shalt have the opportunity of answering for thyself. The most impressive and convincing manner of arguing is allowed to be that by interrogation, which the Almighty here adopts. The best orations delivered by the ancients were formed after this manner. That celebrated oration of Cicero against Catiline, which is allowed to be his masterpiece, begins with a multitude of short questions, closely pressed upon each other. See the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="Job.38.40">Job 38:40</reference> (note).
entries.43f9785e4a5682d1b354ce5700152c93e40ad795: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17852" type="x-p"/> Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? - Thou hast a limited and derived being; thou art only of yesterday; what canst thou know? Didst thou see me create the world?
entries.fd364c3ee77bd2b1b44a2e8f2253c7c11ec88dc6: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17853" type="x-p"/> Who hath laid the measures thereof - Who hath adjusted its polar and equatorial distances from the center? <div eID="gen17853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17854" type="x-p"/> Who hath stretched the line - Who hath formed its zones and its great circles, and adjusted the whole of its magnitude and gravity to the orbit in which it was to move, as well as its distance from that great center about which it was to revolve? These questions show the difficulty of the subject; and that there was an unfathomable depth of counsel and design in the formation of the earth.
entries.9b3f169a24ee4e7ac19e4ef982913494fce8436a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17855" type="x-p"/> Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? - How does it continue to revolve in the immensity of space? What supports it? Has it foundations like a building, and is it fastened with a key-stone, to keep the mighty fabric in union?
entries.db4f46e66008ad78d14fadc673b8891044df38bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17856" type="x-p"/> When the morning stars sang together - This must refer to some intelligent beings who existed before the creation of the visible heavens and earth: and it is supposed that this and the following clause refer to the same beings; that by the sons of God, and the morning stars, the angelic host is meant; as they are supposed to be first, though perhaps not chief, in the order of creation. For the latter clause the Chaldee has, "All the troops of angels." Perhaps their creation may be included in the term heavens, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.1">Gen 1:1</reference> : "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." These witnessed the progress of the creation; and, when God had finished his work, celebrated his wisdom and power in the highest strains.
entries.c6ed8cf7ba75d43cc8a197c5d18e1f22c28cad84: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17857" type="x-p"/> Who shut up the sea with doors - Who gathered the waters together into one place, and fixed the sea its limits, so that it cannot overpass them to inundate the earth? <div eID="gen17857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17858" type="x-p"/> When it brake forth, as if it had issued out of the womb? - This is a very fine metaphor. The sea is represented as a newly born infant issuing from the womb of the void and formless chaos; and the delicate circumstance of the liquor amnii, which bursts out previously to the birth of the foetus, alluded to. The allusion to the birth of a child is carried on in the next verse.
entries.e0643e176ee58a5171d630fcc8b6706183d5f68c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17859" type="x-p"/> When I make the cloud the garment - Alluding to the cloth in which the new-born infant is first received. The cloud was the same to the newly raised vapor, as the above recipient to the new-born child. <div eID="gen17859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17860" type="x-p"/> And thick darkness a swaddlingband for it - Here is also an allusion to the first dressings of the new-born child: it is swathed in order to support the body, too tender to bear even careful handling without some medium between the hand of the nurse and the flesh of the child. "The image," says Mr. Good, "is exquisitely maintained: the new-born ocean is represented as issuing from the womb of chaos; and its dress is that of the new-born infant." There is here an allusion also to the creation, as described in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.1">Gen 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Gen 1:2</reference>. Darkness is there said to be on the face of the Deep. Here it is said, the thick darkness was a swaddlingband for the new-born Sea.
entries.d315ee774940749e2102084ca997ad0929df4098: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17861" type="x-p"/> And brake up for it my decreed place - This refers to the decree, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.9">Gen 1:9</reference> : "Let the waters under the heavens be gathered together unto one place." <div eID="gen17861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17862" type="x-p"/> And set bars and doors - And let the dry land appear. This formed the bars and doors of the sea; the land being everywhere a barrier against the encroachments and inundations of the sea; and great rivers, bays, creeks, etc., the doors by which it passes into the interior of continents, etc.
entries.cd94d006ce079b3b380523be71e6e86f5518bee2: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17863" type="x-p"/> Hitherto shalt thou come - Thus far shall thy flux and reflux extend. The tides are marvellously limited and regulated, not only by the lunar and solar attractions, but by the quantum of time also which is required to remove any part of the earth's surface from under the immediate attractive influence of the sun and moon. And this regulation takes place by means of the rotation of the earth round its own axis, which causes one thousand and forty-two miles of its equator to pass from under any given point in the heavens in one hour; and about five hundred and eighty miles in the latitude of London: so that the attracted fluid parts are every moment passing from under the direct attractive influence, and thus the tides cannot generally be raised to any extraordinary height.
