Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍiḥḥ ,</hi> sunshine, with the former; the latter, whose root is שׂכה (סכה), <hi type="italic">spectare</hi>, is meant to be something that is remarkable in the heavens: an atmospheric phenomenon, a meteor (Hirz.), or a phenomenon caused by light (Ew., Hahn), so that e.g., Umbr. translates: “Who hath put wisdom in the dark clouds, and given understanding to the meteor?” But the meaning which is thus extorted from the words in favour of the connection borders closely upon absurdity. Why, then, shall טחות, from טוּח, Arab. <hi type="italic">ṭı̂ych , oblinere, adipe obducere,</hi> not signify here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.51.8">Psa 51:8</reference>, the reins (embedded in a cushion of fat), and in fact as the seat of the predictive faculty, like כּליות, <reference osisRef="Job.19.27">Job 19:27</reference>, as the seat of the innermost longing for the future; and particularly since here, after the constellations and the influences of the stars have just been spoken of, the mention of the gift of divination is not devoid of connection; and, moreover, as a glance at the next strophe shows, the connection which has been hitherto firmly kept to is already in process of being resolved? <div eID="gen8648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8649" type="x-p"/> If טחות signifies the reins, it is natural to interpret שׂכוי also psychologically, and to translate the intellect (Targ. I, Syr., Arab.), or similarly (Saad., Gecat.), as Ges., Carey, Renan, Schlottm. But there is another rendering handed down which is worthy of attention, although not once mentioned by Rosenm., Hirz., Schlottm., or Hahn, according to which שׂכוי signifies a cock, <hi type="italic">gallum</hi>. We read in <hi type="italic">b. Rosch ha-Schana, </hi> 26 <hi type="italic">a</hi>: ”When I came to Techûm-Kên-Nishraja, R. Simeon b. Lakish relates, the bride was there called נינפי and the cock שׂכוי, according to which <reference osisRef="Job.38.36">Job 38:36</reference> is to be interpreted: שׂכוי = תרנגול.” The Midrash interprets in the same way, <hi type="italic">Jalkut</hi>, §905, beginning: “R. Levi says: In Arabic the cock is called סכוא.” We compare with this, <hi type="italic">Wajikra rabba</hi>, c. 1: “סוכו is Arabic; in Arabia a prophet is called סכוא;” whence it is to be inferred that שׂכוי, as is assumed, describes the cock as a seer, as a prophet. <div eID="gen8649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8650" type="x-p"/> As to the formation of the word, it would certainly be without parallel (Ew., Olsh.) if the word had the tone on the <hi type="italic">penult.,</hi> but Codd. and the best old editions have the <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> by the final syllable; Norzi, who has overlooked this, at least notes שׂכוי with the accent on the <hi type="italic">ult</hi>. as a various reading. It is a secondary noun, Ges. §86, 5, a so-called relative noun (De Sacy, <hi type="italic">Gramm. Arabe</hi>, §768): שׂכרי, <hi type="italic">speculator</hi>, from שׂכו (שׂכוּ, שׂכה), <hi type="italic">speculatio</hi>, as פּלאי, Jdg 13:18 (comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.139.6">Psa 139:6</reference>), <hi type="italic">miraculosus</hi>, from פּלא, a cognate form to the Chald. סכוי (סכואה), of similar meaning. In connection with this primary signification, <hi type="italic">speculator</hi>, it is intelligible how סכוי in Samaritan (vid., Lagarde on Proverbs, S. 62) can signify the eye; here, however, in a Hebrew poet, the cock, of which e.g., Gregory says: <hi type="italic">Speculator semper in altitudine stat, ut quidquid venturum sit longe prospiciat.</hi> That this signification <hi type="italic">speculator</hi> = <hi type="italic">gallus</hi><note placement="foot">No Arab. word offers itself here for comparison: <hi type="italic">tuchaj</hi>, a cock, has different consonants, and if Arab. <hi type="italic">škâ</hi> in the sense of Arab. <hi type="italic">šâk , fortem esse,</hi> were to be supposed, שׂכוי would be a synon. of גּבר, which is likewise a name of the cock.</note> was generally accepted at least in the Talmudic age, the <hi type="italic">Beracha</hi> prescribed to him who hears the cock crow: “Blessed be He who giveth the cock (שׂכוי) knowledge to distinguish between day and night!” shows. In accordance with this, Targ. II translates: who has given understanding לתרנגול בּרא, <hi type="italic">gallo sylvestri</hi> (whereas Targ. I ללבּא, <hi type="italic">cordi, scil. hominis</hi>), to praise his Lord? and Jer.: (<hi type="italic">quis posuit in visceribus hominis sapientiam) et quis dedit gallo intelligentiam</hi>. This traditional rendering, condemned as <hi type="italic">talmudicum commentum</hi> (Ges.), we follow rather than the ”phenomenon” of the moderns who guess at a meaning. What is questioned in Cicero, <hi type="italic">de divin</hi>. ii. 26: <hi type="italic">Quid in mentem venit Callistheni dicere, Deos gallis signum dedisse cantandi, quum id vel natura vel casus efficere potuisset,</hi> Jehovah here claims for Himself. The weather-prophet κατ ̓ ἐξοχήν among animals appropriately appears in this astrologico-meteorological connection by the side of the reins as, according to the Semitic view, a medium of augury (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 268f.). The Koran also makes the cock the watchman who wakes up the heavenly hosts to their duty; and Masius, in his <hi type="italic">Studies of Nature</hi>, has shown how high the cock is placed as being prophetically (for divination) gifted, Moreover, the worship of cocks in the idolatry of the Semites was a service rendered to the stars: the Sabians offered cocks, probably (vid., Chwolsohn, ii. 87) as the white cock of Jezides, regarded by them as a symbol of the sun (<hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenländ. Zeitschr.</hi> 1862, S. 365f.). <div eID="gen8650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8651" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.38.37">Job 38:37</reference></hi> Jerome translates: <hi type="italic">et concentum coelorum quis dormire faciet;</hi> נבלי, however, does not here signify harps, but bottles; and השׁכּיב is not: to lay to rest, but to lay down = to empty, pour out, which the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> also, like the Arab. <hi type="italic">sakaba</hi>, directly signifies. בּצקת might be taken actively: when it pours, but according to 1Ki 22:35 the intransitive rendering is also possible: when the dust pours forth, i.e., flows together, למוּצק, to what is poured out, i.e., not: to the fluid, but in contrast: to a molten mass, i.e., as cast metal (to be explained not according to <reference osisRef="Job.22.16">Job 22:16</reference>, but according to <reference osisRef="Job.37.18">Job 37:18</reference>), for the dry, sandy, dusty earth is made firm by the downfall of the rain (Arab. <hi type="italic">ruṣidat , firmata est terra imbre,</hi> comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">lbbd , pluviam emisit donec arena cohaereret</hi>). רגבים, <hi type="italic">glebae</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Job.21.33">Job 21:33</reference>, from רגב, Arab. <hi type="italic">rjb</hi>, in the primary signification, which as it seems must be supposed: to bring together, from which the significations branch off, to thicken, become firm (<hi type="italic">muraggab</hi>, supported), and to be seized with terror.
entries.2d78c8d31382963e0b1e4f2c1951fed8ee08f225: Job 38:39-41 39  Dost thou hunt for the prey of the lioness <div eID="gen8651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8652" type="x-p"/> And still the desire of the young lions, 40  When they couch in the dens, <div eID="gen8652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8653" type="x-p"/> Sit in the thicket lying in wait for prey? 41  Who provideth for the raven its food, <div eID="gen8653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8654" type="x-p"/> When its young ones cry to God, <div eID="gen8654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8655" type="x-p"/> They wander about without food? <div eID="gen8655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8656" type="x-p"/> On the wealth of the Old Testament language in names for the lion, vid., on Job 4:10. לביא can be used of the lioness; the more exact name of the lioness is לביּה, for לביא is = לבי, whence לבאים, lions, and לבאות, lionesses. The lioness is mentioned first, because she has to provide for her young ones (גּוּרים); then the lions that are still young, but yet are left to themselves, כּפירים. The phrase מלּא חיּה (comp. חיּה of life that needs nourishment, <reference osisRef="Job.33.20">Job 33:20</reference>) is equivalent to מלּא נפשׁ, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.30">Pro 6:30</reference> (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 204 <hi type="italic">ad fin</hi>.). The book of Psalms here furnishes parallels to every word: comp. on <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.38.39">Job 38:39</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.21">Psa 104:21</reference>; on ישׁחוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.10">Psa 10:10</reference>;<note placement="foot">The Semitic is rich in such words as describe the couching posture of beasts of prey lying in wait for their prey, which then in general signify to lie in wait, lurk, wait (רצד, רבץ, Arab. <hi type="italic">rbṣ , lbd , wkkd</hi>); Arab. <hi type="italic">q‛d lh , subsedit ei,</hi> i.e., <hi type="italic">insidiatus est ei,</hi> which corresponds to ישׁבו, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.38.40">Job 38:40</reference></hi>, also belongs here, comp. <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, i. 500 note.</note> on מעונות, <hi type="italic">lustra</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.22">Psa 104:22</reference> (compared on <reference osisRef="Job.37.8">Job 37:8</reference> already); on סכּה, סך, which is used just in the same way, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.9">Psa 10:9</reference>; Jer 25:38. The picture of the crying ravens has its parallel in Psa 147:9. כּי, <hi type="italic">quum</hi>, is followed by the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. in the signif. of the <hi type="italic">praes.,</hi> as Psa 11:3. As here, in the Sermon on the Mount in <reference osisRef="Luke.12.24">Luk 12:24</reference> the ravens, which by their hoarse croaking make themselves most observed everywhere among birds that seek their food, are mentioned instead of the fowls of heaven.  <chapter eID="Job.38"/> <div eID="gen8656" type="x-p"/>

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="38" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXXVIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. THen the LORD answered <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Began to debate the matter with him as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> had desired.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Nah. 1. 3.</ns0:note> out of the whirlwind <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Out of a dark and thick Cloud, from which he sent a ter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rible and tempestuous Wind as the harbinger of his presence. In this manner God appears and speaks to him, partly because this was his usual method in those times, as we see, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19. 18. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 9. 15, 16. See also 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 19. 11. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 1. 4. partly to awaken <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> and his Friends, to the more serious and reverend attention to his words; partly to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>estifie his displeasure both against <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> and against his three Friends, and partly that all of them might be more deeply and throughly humbled and abased within themselves, and prepared the better to receive and longer to retain the instructions which God was about to give them.</ns0:note>, and said,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. Who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">It is a question of admiration and reprehension, What and where is he that presumeth to talk at this rate? This Language be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />comes not a Creature, much less a Professour of Religion. The Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son here designed is not <ns0:hi>Elihu</ns0:hi> who spoke last, but <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> who had spoken most, as is apparent from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. and from Chap. 42. 3. where <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi> takes the following reproof to himself, and from the fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing Discourse wherein God convinceth <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi> by divers of the same kind of arguments which <ns0:hi>Elihu</ns0:hi> had used against him.</ns0:note> that darkeneth counsel <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either 1<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> his own counsel; <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> that expresseth his own mind darkly and doubtful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly. But that was not <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi>'s fault. He spake his mind too plainly and freely. Or rather 2. God's counsel, which is called simply <ns0:hi>coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sel</ns0:hi> by way of eminency, as <ns0:hi>the word</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>the commandment</ns0:hi> are oft put for <ns0:hi>the word</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>command of God.</ns0:hi> For the great matter of the dispute between <ns0:hi>Job,</ns0:hi> and his Friends, was concerning God's counsel, and purpose, and providence in afflicting <ns0:hi>Job;</ns0:hi> which being a wise, and just, and glorious action of God, <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi> had endeavoured to ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scure and misrepresent and censure. And God's decrees and judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments are frequently called his <ns0:hi>counsels,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 33. 11. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 19. 21. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 28. 29. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 2. 23.</ns0:note> by words <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">God doth not charge <ns0:hi>Job,</ns0:hi> as his three Friends had done, with hypocrisie and wickedness in the course of life, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>or with atheistical opinions of God, or his providence, as some of the Hebrew Writers do, but confines, his reproof to his hard speeches.</ns0:note> without knowledge <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Proceeding from ignorance, and mistake, and inconsi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derateness; not from malice or rage against God, as his Friends accused him.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 40. 7.</ns0:note> Gird up now thy loins <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">As Warriours then did for the Battle. Prepare thy self for the Combate with me, which thou hast oft desired. I accept of thy Challenge, Ch. 13. 22. and elsewhere.</ns0:note> like a man; for I will demand of thee <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>I will ask thee Questions;</ns0:hi> which he doth in the following Verses.</ns0:note> and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> make me know.</ns0:note> answer thou me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 104. 5. Prov. 8. 29, & 30. 4.</ns0:note> Where wast thou <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Then thou wast no where, thou hadst no being; thou art but of yesterday; and dost thou presume to judge of my eternal Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sels! I made the World without thy help, and therefore can go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vern it without thy counsel, and I do not need thee to be the Controller or Censu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>er of my works.</ns0:note>, when I laid the foundati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons of the earth <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">When I made the Earth, which is as the Foundation or lower part of the whole World, and settled it as firm and fast upon its own Center as if it had been built upon the surest Foundations.</ns0:note>? declare, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> if thou knowest under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing.</ns0:note> if thou hast understanding <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">But if thou art ignorant of these manifest and visible works, do not pretend to the exact knowledge of my secret Counsels and mysterious Providences.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. Who hath laid the measures thereof <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Who hath prescribed how long and broad and deep it should be.</ns0:note>, if thou knowest? or who hath stretched the line <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To wit, the measuring line to regulate all its dimensions, so as might be most convenient<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> both for beauty and use.</ns0:note> upon it?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. Whereupon are the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> foundations thereof <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> made to si<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>k.</ns0:note> fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stened <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">This strong and durable Building hath no Foundations but in God's power and word which hath marvellously established it up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on it self.</ns0:note>? or who laid the corner stone thereof <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">By which the several walls and parts of the Building are joyned and fastened together, and in which, next to the Foun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dations, the stability of any Building does consist. The sense is, Who was it that did build this goodly Fabrick, and establish<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> it so firmly that it cannot be moved without a Miracle.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. When the morning stars <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either 1. the Stars properly so called, who are said to sing and praise God, objectively, because they give men ample occasion to do it in regard of their glorious light and stupendious motions, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Compare <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 19. 1. & 148, 1, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> But, 1. there stars are not here the objects or matter, but the authors or instruments of God's praises for the founding of the Earth. 2. the Stars were not created when the Earth was founded, but upon the fourth day. 3. there is no satisfactory reason given why all the Stars should be called <ns0:hi>Morning<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stars,</ns0:hi> especially when there is but one Star known by that Name. Or rather 2. the Sons of God, as it here follows, the latter Clause of the Verse being explicatory of the former, as is most frequent in this and some other Books of Scripture, to wit, the Angels, who may well be called <ns0:hi>Stars</ns0:hi> as even men of eminent note, and particu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ly Ministers of God's Word are called. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 8. 10. & 12. 3. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 1. 16, 20. and <ns0:hi>Morning-stars,</ns0:hi> because of their excellent lustre and glory, for which they are called <ns0:hi>Angels of Light,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11. 14. and Christ for the same reason is called <ns0:hi>the Morning-star,</ns0:hi> Revel. 22. 16.</ns0:note> sang together, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, so Or.</ns0:note> and all the sons of God <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The blessed Angels; for man not being yet made, God had then no other Sons; and these are called <ns0:hi>the Sons of God,</ns0:hi> partly be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they had their whole being from him, and partly because they were made partakers of his divine and glorious Image. And <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> these are said to join in this work of praising God, probably be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause none of the Angels were as yet fallen from their first estate, though they did <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>all within a very little time after.</ns0:note> shouted for joy <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Rejoyced in and blessed God for his works. Whereby he intimates, that they neither did advise or any way assist him in his works, nor dislike or censure any of his works, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> had presumed to do with the works of his Providence, which are not inferior to those of Creation.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 1. 9.</ns0:note> Or <ns0:hi>who</ns0:hi> shut up the sea with doors <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Who was it, thou or I, that did set bounds to the vast and raging Ocean, and shut it up as it were with Doors within its proper place and store-house that it might not overflow the Earth; which without God's powerful restraint it would do? See <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 33. 7. & 104. 9. This sense seems most proper and to be confirmed by the fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing Verses.</ns0:note>, when it brake forth <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>after it had broken forth,</ns0:hi> to it, from the womb or bowels of the Earth, within which the Waters were for the most part contained, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 1. 2. Compare 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3. 5. and out of which they were by God's command brought forth into the proper place or channel which God had appointed for them.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>as if it</ns0:hi> had issued out of the womb.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. When I made the cloud the garment thereof <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">When I covered it with Vapours and Clouds which arise out of the Sea, and by God's appointment hover above it and cover it like a garment.</ns0:note>, and thick darkness <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Black and dark Clouds, called <ns0:hi>Darkness</ns0:hi> by an usual Metonymy of the Adjunct. So the same thing is repeated in other words after the manner.</ns0:note> a swadling band for it <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Having compared the Sea to a New-born Infant he continues in the same Metaphor, and makes the Clouds as swadling-bands to keep the Sea within its bounds: though indeed neither Clouds, nor Air, nor Sands, and shores, can bound the Sea, but it is God alone who doth it in and with these things.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. And <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 span">
                           <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 26. 10.</ns0:note> brake up for it my decreed <ns0:hi>place</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
